performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: Cold gets into the strings: first a shiver, then stamping feet and chattering teeth. Between them the solo violin sends gusts of demisemiquavers across the orchestra.

sections.label: A · Shivering strings
sections.mNote: Repeated notes gather from the bass upwards; the violin adds trills

sections.label: B · The violin’s bitter wind
sections.mNote: Rapid broken chords interrupt the shivering

sections.label: A′ · Shivering turns to stamping
sections.mNote: Repeated quavers tighten into semiquavers and demisemiquavers

sections.label: C · Solo runs and orchestral gusts
sections.mNote: The violin travels from F minor towards E♭ major

sections.label: A″ · Shivering in E♭ major
sections.mNote: The strings return with the refrain’s repeated notes

sections.label: D · The violin chatters its teeth
sections.mNote: Repeated semiquavers carry the solo back towards F minor

sections.label: A′ · Stamping in F minor
sections.mNote: The full strings repeat the stamping music to close

cues.title: Cold from the ground up
cues.text: “Aggiacciato tremar trà nevi algenti” — “To shiver, frozen, among icy snows.” The 1725 sonnet starts with a body in the cold. Repeated string notes build upwards from the bass; the solo violin joins with a trill on each short note.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, letter A; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, I, bars 1–11: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351. The sonnets were published anonymously with Op. 8.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bitter wind
cues.text: “Al Severo Spirar d’orrido Vento” — “In the harsh breath of a dreadful wind.” The solo violin breaks into demisemiquavers, leaping through broken chords and racing down scales. Short orchestral interruptions bring back the shivering.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter B; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 12–18, solo marked Orrido Vento: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Feet against the cold
cues.text: “Correr battendo i piedi ogni momento” — “To run, stamping one’s feet at every moment.” Vivaldi squeezes the repeated notes closer together. Semiquavers sprout little bursts of demisemiquavers: the shivering body is trying to warm itself.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter C; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 20–26; the stamping inscription begins halfway through bar 22: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Faster than a copyist
cues.text: In Venice in 1739 Charles de Brosses writes home: “Vivaldi has become one of my intimate friends, to sell me concertos very dear.” The old man, he adds, has a prodigious fury for composing, and boasts that he can write a concerto, with all its parts, faster than a copyist can copy one.
cues.evidence: Charles de Brosses, letter XVIII to M. de Blancey, 29 August (1739), Lettres familières écrites d’Italie (ed. Hippolyte Babou, Poulet-Malassis et de Broise, 1858, vol. 1, pp. 141–148): “Vivaldi s’est fait de mes amis intimes, pour me vendre des concertos bien chers”, “une furie de composition prodigieuse”, and “plus promptement qu’un copiste ne le pourroit copier”; translation ours. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Lettres_famili%C3%A8res_%C3%A9crites_d%E2%80%99Italie_T.1/%C3%80_M._DE_BLANCEY._%E2%80%94_Suite_du_s%C3%A9jour_%C3%A0_Venise

cues.title: Teeth in the bow
cues.text: “E pel Soverchio gel batter i denti” — “And to chatter one’s teeth from the excessive frost.” The solo violin repeats short notes under the words Batter li denti. The teeth keep chattering while the harmony passes through A♭ major and C minor towards F minor.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter D; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 47–56; harmonic route in José Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: One last stamp
cues.text: The full strings take over in F minor. Vivaldi brings back the stamping part of the refrain, with its rapid repeated notes, and drives it to the final cadence. The movement ends on its feet.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 56–63, final ritornello; its use of the stamping music is identified at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: A C-minor gust
transitions.how: The shivering passage moves from F minor to C minor. The solo violin begins the wind on C, leaping an octave before racing through the notes of a C-minor chord. The orchestra interrupts with short returns of the shivering rhythm; the Allegro non molto marking remains.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 9–18; key change discussed at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: The shiver becomes a stamp
transitions.how: The wind returns to F minor and the full strings resume the repeated-note refrain. At bar 20 the violin turns its short quavers into semiquavers on F. Demisemiquaver bursts then break into that pulse under the inscription about running and stamping feet.

transitions.title: The violin runs out of F minor
transitions.to: C · Solo runs and orchestral gusts
transitions.how: The stamping strings release the soloist in F minor. Its demisemiquavers wind around F, E♮ and G before climbing higher. The orchestra keeps the shivering figure beneath it, then interrupts with bursts marked winds as the episode travels towards E♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 26–38; orchestral wind interruptions and E♭-major destination described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: The strings shiver in E♭
transitions.from: C · Solo runs and orchestral gusts
transitions.how: The solo episode reaches E♭ major. The full strings bring back the repeated-note refrain in that key, including its semiquaver version. Vivaldi saves the denser stamping figures for the final return in F minor.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 38–44; the refrain’s contents are identified at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: The solo begins to chatter
transitions.to: D · The violin chatters its teeth
transitions.how: The soloist leaves the E♭-major refrain and begins another rapid passage. At bar 47 repeated semiquavers carry the inscription Batter li denti. The episode passes through A♭ major and C minor before reaching F minor for the last tutti.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 44–56; harmonic itinerary at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: F minor under stamping feet
transitions.from: D · The violin chatters its teeth
transitions.how: The solo episode reaches F minor and the full strings take up the stamping music. Rapid repeated notes alternate with broken chords. The final refrain keeps this denser part of the earlier tutti through to the F-minor cadence.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 56–63; final ritornello described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: I. Allegro non molto; opening staggered entries, solo passages and ritornellos. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

composer.epithet: He wrote concertos for the women of Venice’s Pietà, operas for its theatres, and a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 a twenty-five-year-old Venetian became a priest in March and a violin teacher in September. Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and continued helping with his career long after the son had become famous. Venice knew Antonio as il prete rosso, the red priest. His working places would be the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year: in 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 took him back. The music survived the office politics.
